# What this document does

Dan Simon is presenting the retribution study at Princeton and is building his
own slides. This document draws the graphics he asked for, one per slide, so
that each can be dropped onto a blank 16:9 slide. It answers three requests.

**1. Revenge against desert, just deserts, and severity-deserts.** The paper
compares revenge with desert theory (H9 and H10). Dan asked whether the proper
comparison is with just deserts, and proposed a new score, **severity-deserts**,
that averages desert theory with the severity index. Slides 1 to 4 set revenge
beside all three desert-based scores: how much participants endorsed each
(slide 1), how closely each goes with punitiveness in the whole sample
(slide 2) and among retributivists (slide 4), and how the parts of the two
composites go with punitiveness on their own (slide 3), which shows why
averaging in proportionality lowers just deserts and averaging in severity
raises severity-deserts. The statistical tests of these comparisons are
written to a table (`princeton_talk_tests.csv`), not drawn.

**2. Two models of agency.** Retributivists scored higher than the
participants who ranked deterrence or incapacitation first on essentialism
about offenders, on the belief that crime is a choice, and on rejecting
society's responsibility for crime. Dan suggested reading these as one view of
agency, **agency as blameworthiness**, which predicts exactly those
differences, and setting it against **agency as benevolence**, the view that
retributivism rests on respect for the offender's dignity, which predicts that
retributivists would be no more hateful and no more willing to degrade, to
inflict suffering, or to impose harsh conditions. Slide 5 shows both sets of
differences, grouped by the model that speaks to them. No new test is run: the
differences are the paper's (Table S19, last column).

**3. The four ways of identifying retributivists.** Dan asked for the graphic
showing the registered contrasts under all four groupings (the ranking, the
median split, the top and bottom thirds, and the sentencing ratio). Slide 6
redraws it on the paper's scorings, and slide 7 summarizes it, one bar per
grouping. Under the ranking, slides 6 and 7 compare retributivists with all
577 other participants, the registered comparison; slide 5, like the paper's
main text, compares them with the 453 who ranked deterrence or incapacitation
first. The same measure therefore has a larger d on slide 6 than on slide 5
(essentialism 0.69 against 0.59), and the ranking's median d is 0.51 against
all others and 0.41 against the 453.

**Slides 8 to 11, and the main line of the talk.** The recommended main line
of the talk is **slides 8, 9, 10 and 6**, four plain slides that carry the
argument; slides 1 to 5, 7 and 11 are backups for questions.

- **Slide 8, "Endorsing and Punishing."** Revenge, desert theory and the
  proportionality principle, each twice: the share of participants who agree
  with it (a mean above the neutral 4) and how closely it goes with
  punitiveness. It shows that the principle almost everyone accepts (83.1%)
  has almost nothing to do with punishing (r = .038).
- **Slide 9, "Revenge, Desert, and Punitiveness."** The correlations of
  slides 2 and 4 on one slide: the four scores' correlations with
  punitiveness in the whole sample and among retributivists, side by side.
  Its header says who the retributivists are, because it is the first slide
  of the main line that names them.
- **Slide 10, "Two Models of Agency."** Slide 5 told in shares rather than
  in Cohen's d: the percentage of retributivists, and of those who ranked
  deterrence or incapacitation first, who endorse each of the seven measures
  (a mean above 4, the scale midpoint).
- **Slide 11, "Revenge and Desert, Three Ways"** (backup). The correlations
  of revenge (its four items, and Study 1's three items), desert theory,
  just deserts and severity-deserts with punitiveness, with the
  policy-and-sentence components alone, and with the first sentence alone,
  for the question whether revenge's lead depends on the attitude
  components.

**Slides 12 to 14: two questions Dan asked about numbers in the paper.**

- **Slide 12, "Desert, Proportionality, and Severity."** The paper gives
  desert theory's correlations with the proportionality principle and with
  the severity index twice: r = .199 and .474 (Results, Part 2, H6) and
  r = .078 and .277 (Part 3, H11). The first pair is the whole sample, the
  second the 371 retributivists alone. The slide sets the two pairs side by
  side, one panel per sample. In both, desert theory goes more closely with
  the severity index than with the principle. Among retributivists both
  correlations are lower, partly because the retributivists' desert-theory
  scores are bunched near the top of the scale (their SD is 0.83, against
  1.19 in the whole sample), and a score that varies less can correlate less
  with anything.
- **Slide 13, "Sentences by Group."** The first and second sentences, in
  years, of the retributivists and of all 577 other participants, with each
  group's mean, median, and share choosing the 50-year maximum. The
  registered test of the first sentence (H14) is in the caption.
- **Slide 14, "First Sentence by First-Ranked Goal"** (backup). The first
  sentence of each of the four groups defined by the goal of punishment
  ranked first. The 577 non-retributivists are not one group: those who
  ranked rehabilitation first gave the shortest sentences.

Severity-deserts is marked as new and exploratory wherever it appears (a
white bar with a black outline on slides 2, 4, 9 and 11, and in its label on
slide 1). The desert bars are a mid gray that holds up on a projector.
Slide 6 draws no intervals, so that its 79 bars stay legible; the caption
gives their typical half-width, and a dashed line marks each grouping's
median d.

**Design.** Every slide is 16:9 and in grayscale, with a short centered title
and a caption of one or two lines. Correlations, differences, shares and
summaries are bar charts; the 1-to-7 scores are violin plots. The takeaway of
each slide is left to the speaker.

**What is new here and what is not.** Severity-deserts is new: it was not
preregistered and is not in the paper, and every result that uses it is
exploratory. The grouping of measures under the two models of agency is also
new and ours. So are, on slide 8, the shares agreeing with revenge and with
desert theory; on slide 10, the three blameworthiness shares and every
comparison of shares; and on slide 11, the policy-and-sentence outcome and
every correlation outside the first panel (except the .549 of revenge on
Study 1's three items, which the Supplement reports). On slide 12 the
retributivists' SD of desert theory and the 95% CIs of the retributivists'
two correlations are new (the paper prints the two r's and their
difference). On slides 13 and 14 every number in years is new and
descriptive: the group means, medians, SDs, and shares choosing 50; the paper
reports the whole-sample sentences, the registered H14 test on the
standardized first sentence, and, in Table S20, the four goal groups'
standardized means. Each of these new
numbers is guarded against its value computed independently of this
document, so the knit stops if a later edit moves it. Every other
number on the slides is a number already in the paper or in an export of
`01_main_analysis.Rmd`, and a guard checks each one against its source; the
knit stops if any guard fails.

**Reads.** Study 2's scored data and the tables `01_main_analysis.Rmd`
exported. Nothing here changes the analysis.

**Writes.** Fourteen figures, each as PNG (for slides) and PDF (for print), to
`output/figures/princeton_talk/`, with a copy of each PNG in
`Docs/Writing/figures/princeton_talk/`. Two tables:
`output/tables/princeton_talk_figure_values.csv`, every value each slide
plots (and, for slide 10, the tests of its differences; for slide 12, the
differences between its correlations and the SDs; for slides 13 and 14, the
medians, SDs, shares choosing 50, and who reduced, kept, or raised the
sentence), and
`output/tables/princeton_talk_tests.csv`, the tests of dependent correlations
and paired differences behind slides 1 to 4, 9 and 11.

**Run order.** Knit `01_main_analysis.Rmd` first. This document reads its
exports and stops if any is missing.

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# === SETUP ===
# echo = TRUE so every computation is visible in the knitted report, as in the
# other documents in this folder. message and warning are silenced only for
# package start-up chatter. Everything that matters is a stopifnot() guard or a
# same() guard, which halts the knit, so nothing depends on a warning being seen.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center")
```

# 1. Paths, packages, and inputs

```{r paths}
# === PATHS AND INPUT CHECKS ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: names every input and output, loads the packages, reads
# the scored data, and stops if any export the figures need is missing.
# READS: data/cleaned/retribution_scored.rds and the exports listed below.
# WRITES: nothing yet; it only creates the two figure folders and clears this
#         document's own old slides from them.
#
# PATHS ARE RELATIVE to this document's folder, like the other documents here,
# so the file runs unchanged wherever the project folder sits.
S2_TABLES   <- file.path("output", "tables")
S2_DATA     <- file.path("data", "cleaned", "retribution_scored.rds")
OUT_FIGURES <- file.path("output", "figures", "princeton_talk")
OUT_TABLES  <- file.path("output", "tables")
# A copy of every PNG goes to the manuscript's figure folder, beside the paper's
# own figures and the earlier talk figures, so everything Dan might paste into a
# deck sits in one place.
DOCS_FIG    <- file.path("..", "..", "Docs", "Writing", "figures", "princeton_talk")
dir.create(OUT_FIGURES, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(DOCS_FIG, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
# CLEAR THIS DOCUMENT'S OLD SLIDES FIRST. Every file named pt_*.png or pt_*.pdf
# in these two folders is written by this document and nothing else. Removing
# them before drawing means a slide dropped or renamed in a later version cannot
# linger beside the current set and be mistaken for part of it.
# DANGER: keep the "^pt_" anchor. Widening this pattern would delete the
# paper's figures or the Study 2 talk figures (s2_*), which other documents
# write into neighbouring folders.
unlink(list.files(OUT_FIGURES, pattern = "^pt_.*\\.(png|pdf)$", full.names = TRUE))
unlink(list.files(DOCS_FIG, pattern = "^pt_.*\\.png$", full.names = TRUE))

# Every export read below. A missing file means 01_main_analysis.Rmd has not
# been knitted since the section that writes it was added; knit it first.
#   PAPER_person_scores      the paper's scores, one row per participant (9.19A, 9.19G)
#   PAPER_H9, PAPER_JD_H9    H9 on the paper's scorings (paired endorsement)
#   PAPER_H11_H9, PAPER_JD_H11_H9   the same among retributivists (H11)
#   PAPER_H10, PAPER_H10_cors, PAPER_JD_H10, PAPER_JD_H10_cors   H10 and its r's
#   PAPER_H11_H10, PAPER_H11_H10_cors, PAPER_JD_H11_H10   H10 among retributivists
#   PAPER_H6                 punitiveness with the severity index and the principle
#   PAPER_JD_parts           means of the two parts of just deserts
#   PAPER_contrasts_*        the registered contrasts under each grouping, and
#                            the main text's comparison with the deterrence- or
#                            incapacitation-first
#   PAPER_scorecard          the counts and medians Table S16 reports
#   H4_shares                the share agreeing with the proportionality
#                            principle (slide 8; Results, Part 2, H4: 83.1%)
#   H12_retributivist_endorsement, PAPER_H12_shares_vs_deter_incap
#                            the shares endorsing each hostile attitude among
#                            retributivists and among the deterrence- or
#                            incapacitation-first (slide 10; H12, Figure 11)
#   PAPER_H6_cors, PAPER_H11_H6, PAPER_H11_H6_steiger
#                            desert theory with the principle and with the
#                            severity index, whole sample and retributivists,
#                            and the difference among retributivists (slide 12;
#                            H6 in Parts 2 and 3). PAPER_H6, above, holds the
#                            whole-sample difference.
#   PAPER_reliability        the SD of desert theory in the whole sample
#                            (slide 12; Table 1)
#   descriptives             the whole sample's mean first sentence (slide 13)
#   P3_sentence_direction_by_ranking
#                            who reduced, kept, or raised the sentence, by the
#                            ranking grouping (slide 13; Supplement, Panel C of
#                            the groupings figure)
#   first_choice_group_means the standardized first sentence of each
#                            first-ranked-goal group (slide 14; Table S20)
S2_NEEDED <- c("PAPER_person_scores", "PAPER_H9", "PAPER_JD_H9", "PAPER_H11_H9",
               "PAPER_JD_H11_H9", "PAPER_H10", "PAPER_H10_cors", "PAPER_JD_H10",
               "PAPER_JD_H10_cors", "PAPER_H11_H10", "PAPER_H11_H10_cors",
               "PAPER_JD_H11_H10", "PAPER_H6", "PAPER_JD_parts",
               "PAPER_contrasts_vs_deter_incap", "PAPER_contrasts_rank",
               "PAPER_contrasts_med", "PAPER_contrasts_tert",
               "PAPER_contrasts_ratio", "PAPER_scorecard", "H4_shares",
               "H12_retributivist_endorsement", "PAPER_H12_shares_vs_deter_incap",
               "PAPER_H6_cors", "PAPER_H11_H6", "PAPER_H11_H6_steiger",
               "PAPER_reliability", "descriptives",
               "P3_sentence_direction_by_ranking", "first_choice_group_means")
S2_MISSING <- S2_NEEDED[!file.exists(file.path(S2_TABLES,
                                               paste0(S2_NEEDED, ".csv")))]
if (length(S2_MISSING)) stop("Knit 01_main_analysis.Rmd first. Missing: ",
                             paste(S2_MISSING, collapse = ", "))
stopifnot(file.exists(S2_DATA))

library(ggplot2)
# effectsize and cocor are called with :: below, exactly as 01 calls them, so
# the effect sizes and the dependent-correlation tests are computed by the same
# code that produced the paper's numbers. Stop here, with a clear message,
# rather than halfway through a figure if either is missing.
for (pkg in c("effectsize", "cocor"))
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) stop("Install the package ", pkg)

d <- as.data.frame(readRDS(S2_DATA))
read_s2 <- function(name) read.csv(file.path(S2_TABLES, paste0(name, ".csv")),
                                   stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
stopifnot(nrow(d) == 948)
cat(sprintf("Study 2: %d participants.\n", nrow(d)))
```

# 2. Shared tools: style, grays, intervals, and a guard

```{r tools}
# === ONE STYLE FOR EVERY SLIDE ===
# SLIDE SIZE. 13.333 x 7.5 inches is the standard 16:9 PowerPoint and Keynote
# slide, so a figure dropped onto a blank slide fills it at full size and the
# type prints at the size set here. PNGs are written at 200 dpi (2667 x 1500
# pixels), sharp on a projector without making the files large.
SLIDE_W <- 13.333; SLIDE_H <- 7.5; SLIDE_DPI <- 200

# GRAYSCALE. Every slide uses grays only, so the figures read the same on any
# projector, in print, and to a viewer who cannot tell colours apart. When a
# slide compares categories, they are told apart by shade, and every shade is
# also named in a legend or by a label on the bar itself.
# The four data grays form one light-to-dark ramp. The data-visualization
# palette validator confirmed that each step is visibly darker than the one
# before it and that the lightest still stands out against the white slide.
G1 <- "#1a1a1a"   # darkest: the series the slide is about
G2 <- "#404040"
G3 <- "#737373"
G4 <- "#b0b0b0"   # lightest data gray
# Two evenly spaced ramps for stacked bars, where neighbouring segments touch
# and must be told apart at a glance (also validated, light to dark):
RAMP4 <- c("#1a1a1a", "#4f4f4f", "#808080", "#b0b0b0")   # 1st to 4th place
RAMP3 <- c("#b0b0b0", "#666666", "#1a1a1a")              # reduced, kept, raised
FILL_VIOLIN <- "#d9d9d9"   # violin bodies: light, so the mean marks stand out
INK   <- "#000000"   # titles and values
INK2  <- "#404040"   # axis text
MUTED <- "#7a7a7a"   # reference lines only (the dashed neutral line)
# CAPTIONS take a darker gray than the reference lines. #7a7a7a on white is a
# contrast of about 4.3 to 1, below the 4.5 to 1 minimum for small text, and
# washes out on a projector; #555555 is about 7.5 to 1 and still reads as
# secondary to the black titles and values.
CAP_INK <- "#555555"
GRID  <- "#e6e6e6"   # hairline gridlines
BAND  <- "#eeeeee"   # shaded reference band

theme_slide <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 20, base_family = "sans") +
    theme(text = element_text(colour = INK),
          # SHORT, CENTERED TITLES. hjust = 0.5 centers the title; with
          # plot.title.position = "plot" it is centered on the whole slide,
          # not just on the plotting area.
          plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 30, hjust = 0.5,
                                    margin = margin(b = 18)),
          # 14 pt in CAP_INK: the largest size at which every caption still
          # fits on two lines at the wrap width cap() uses below.
          plot.caption = element_text(size = 14, colour = CAP_INK, hjust = 0.5,
                                      margin = margin(t = 16), lineheight = 1.1),
          plot.title.position = "plot", plot.caption.position = "plot",
          axis.text = element_text(colour = INK2, size = 18),
          axis.title = element_text(colour = INK2, size = 18),
          axis.title.x = element_text(margin = margin(t = 10)),
          axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(r = 10)),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "center",
          legend.title = element_blank(),
          legend.text = element_text(size = 18, colour = INK2),
          legend.key.size = unit(1.1, "lines"),
          plot.margin = margin(26, 40, 18, 30))
}
# Horizontal bars: gridlines run up the value axis only.
theme_hbar <- function() theme_slide() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = GRID, linewidth = 0.5),
        axis.text.y = element_text(colour = INK, size = 19))
# Vertical bars and violins: gridlines run across the value axis only.
theme_vbar <- function() theme_slide() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_line(colour = GRID, linewidth = 0.5),
        axis.text.x = element_text(colour = INK, size = 19))

# Correlations print without the leading zero (.71, not 0.71), as in the paper,
# and negative values take a true minus sign. A correlation smaller than .01 in
# size would print as .00 or .01 at two decimals, which misstates it, so it gets
# three decimals (.007).
fmt_r <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  dg <- ifelse(abs(x) < 0.01, 3, digits)
  s <- vapply(seq_along(x), function(i) formatC(x[i], format = "f", digits = dg[i]),
              character(1))
  s <- sub("^(-?)0\\.", "\\1.", s)
  sub("^-", "−", s)
}
# AXIS TICKS FOR r, one decimal without the leading zero (.2, .4), except
# zero itself, which prints as "0": ".0" reads as a typo on a slide. The
# !is.na() keeps a missing break (ggplot2 passes NA for a break outside the
# panel) from breaking the assignment.
axis_r <- function(x) {
  s <- sub("^-", "−", sub("^(-?)0\\.", "\\1.", sprintf("%.1f", x)))
  s[!is.na(x) & abs(x) < 1e-9] <- "0"
  s
}
# CAPTIONS: each argument to cap() is one line of the caption, written as a
# phrase or sentence that is whole on its own. Each argument is wrapped on its
# own, so a line break falls where the writer put it, between two phrases,
# never in the middle of one ("Error / bars"), which is hard to take in from
# the back of a hall. 140 characters is the width of the slide at the 14-pt
# caption size set above, so a line up to that length stays on the slide.
# GUARD: a caption that would take three lines stops the knit, naming its
# first line, so an overlong argument is shortened rather than silently
# broken mid-phrase.
# DANGER: raising the caption size without lowering this width lets a line
# run past the slide's edge; lowering the width without shortening a caption
# can push it to three lines. Look at every PNG after changing either.
cap <- function(...) {
  lines <- unlist(lapply(c(...), strwrap, width = 140))
  if (length(lines) > 2) stop("Caption runs to ", length(lines), " lines: ", lines[1])
  paste(lines, collapse = "\n")
}

# PEARSON r WITH ITS 95% INTERVAL. cor.test() gives the Fisher-z interval, the
# interval the main analysis uses for every correlation.
cor_ci <- function(x, y) {
  tt <- cor.test(x, y)
  data.frame(r = unname(tt$estimate), lower = tt$conf.int[1],
             upper = tt$conf.int[2], n = sum(complete.cases(x, y)))
}
# A 95% interval for a mean.
mean_ci <- function(x) {
  tt <- t.test(x)
  data.frame(mean = mean(x), lower = tt$conf.int[1], upper = tt$conf.int[2],
             n = length(x))
}
# GUARD: two numbers must agree to within a tolerance, or the knit stops with a
# message naming the check.
# HOW IT COMPARES. all.equal() measures ONE mean relative difference over the
# whole vector (the summed absolute differences over the summed absolute
# targets), and switches to an absolute difference when the target is smaller
# than the tolerance. So a vector that mixes sizes (a t of 7 beside a p of
# 1e-12) checks the small entries hardly at all. Guards on a group of numbers
# of different sizes therefore use same_each() below, and p-values use
# same_p(), never this function.
same <- function(a, b, what, tol = 1e-8) {
  if (!isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(a), as.numeric(b), tolerance = tol)))
    stop("Guard failed: ", what, " (", paste(signif(a, 6), collapse = ", "),
         " vs ", paste(signif(b, 6), collapse = ", "), ")")
  invisible(TRUE)
}

# EVERY PLOTTED VALUE is collected here and written to one table at the end.
VALUES <- list()
keep_values <- function(fig, df) VALUES[[fig]] <<- cbind(figure = fig, df)

# THE PDF DEVICE, as in 04_two_study_figures.Rmd. R's default pdf() device draws
# every hyphen as a long minus sign ("Second-Degree" prints as "Second−Degree"),
# cannot encode Greek letters, and does not embed its fonts. On a Mac the slides
# are drawn with the system's own quartz PDF device, which has none of these
# faults; elsewhere cairo_pdf(), which also prints real hyphens and embeds its
# fonts. The title argument names each PDF after its file.
PDF_DEVICE <- if (capabilities("aqua")) {
  function(filename, width, height, bg = "white", ...)
    grDevices::quartz(type = "pdf", file = filename, width = width, height = height, bg = bg,
                      title = tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(filename)))
} else {
  grDevices::cairo_pdf
}
save_slide <- function(p, name) {
  png_path <- file.path(OUT_FIGURES, paste0(name, ".png"))
  ggsave(png_path, p, width = SLIDE_W, height = SLIDE_H, dpi = SLIDE_DPI,
         bg = "white")
  ggsave(file.path(OUT_FIGURES, paste0(name, ".pdf")), p,
         width = SLIDE_W, height = SLIDE_H, bg = "white", device = PDF_DEVICE)
  file.copy(png_path, file.path(DOCS_FIG, basename(png_path)), overwrite = TRUE)
}

# HORIZONTAL BAR CHART OF CORRELATIONS, used by several slides. One bar per
# row, the value printed past the end of its interval. `fill` names the column
# that sets each bar's gray; `dodge` > 0 sets two bars per row side by side.
# coord_cartesian() zooms the axis without dropping any interval that runs past
# its ends (scale limits would silently delete such an interval).
bar_r <- function(df, y, fill, fills, xlim, xbreaks, xlab, dodge = 0) {
  pos <- if (dodge > 0) position_dodge(width = dodge) else position_identity()
  ggplot(df, aes(x = r, y = .data[[y]], fill = .data[[fill]])) +
    geom_col(width = if (dodge > 0) dodge * 0.95 else 0.68, position = pos) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), width = 0.22,
                  orientation = "y", linewidth = 0.7, colour = INK, position = pos) +
    geom_text(aes(x = pmax(upper, 0) + 0.012, label = fmt_r(r)), hjust = 0,
              size = 6, colour = INK, position = pos, show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = INK2, linewidth = 0.6) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = fills) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = xbreaks, labels = axis_r) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = xlim, clip = "off") +
    labs(x = xlab, y = NULL) +
    theme_hbar()
}

# VIOLIN PLOT OF 1-TO-7 SCORES, used by slide 1. The violin is the shape of
# everyone's answers (wider where more people answered); the black point is
# the mean and the black bar its 95% interval; the dashed line is the neutral
# midpoint of the scale.
# THE SCALE LABELS sit on one line each, with the anchor word before the
# numeral ("Strongly agree  7"), so every numeral is level with its own
# gridline. A label stacked over several lines ("7" above "Strongly agree") is
# centred on its gridline as a block, which lifts the numeral above the line
# it names.
violin_1to7 <- function(long, stats, x_levels) {
  long$measure  <- factor(long$measure, levels = x_levels)
  stats$measure <- factor(stats$measure, levels = x_levels)
  ggplot(long, aes(x = measure, y = score)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 4, linetype = "dashed", colour = MUTED, linewidth = 0.6) +
    geom_violin(fill = FILL_VIOLIN, colour = G3, linewidth = 0.6, width = 0.85,
                scale = "width", adjust = 1.2, trim = TRUE) +
    # EACH POINT IS ONE PARTICIPANT, spread sideways at random so that people
    # with the same score do not sit on top of one another. The spread is
    # sideways only, so every point stays at the participant's score; the seed
    # fixes the spread, so every knit draws the same slide.
    geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.22, height = 0, seed = 1),
               size = 1.1, alpha = 0.3, colour = G3, stroke = 0) +
    geom_errorbar(data = stats, aes(x = measure, ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
                  inherit.aes = FALSE, width = 0.12, linewidth = 1, colour = INK) +
    geom_point(data = stats, aes(x = measure, y = mean), inherit.aes = FALSE,
               size = 5, colour = INK) +
    geom_label(data = stats, aes(x = measure, y = mean, label = sprintf("%.2f", mean)),
               inherit.aes = FALSE, nudge_x = 0.2, hjust = 0, size = 6,
               label.size = 0, fill = "white", label.padding = unit(0.15, "lines")) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:7, limits = c(1, 7),
                       labels = c("Strongly disagree  1", "2", "3", "Neutral  4",
                                  "5", "6", "Strongly agree  7")) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_vbar() +
    theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 17))
}
```

```{r tools_talk}
# === TOOLS THIS DOCUMENT ADDS ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: defines the helpers the shared tools above do not have:
# a guard against numbers printed in the paper, a formatter for Cohen's d, a
# white knock-out that keeps intervals visible inside dark bars, a bar chart
# of d, and three statistical helpers that repeat, line for line, the
# way 01_main_analysis.Rmd computes a group contrast (welch_contrast()), a
# paired comparison (paired_test()), and a comparison of two dependent
# correlations (steiger_overlap()). Repeating 01's code rather than writing new
# code is what lets every guard below demand agreement to 1e-8.
# For slides 8 to 11 it also defines, at the end of this chunk: an outline
# rule for white bars (edge_of()), a faceted bar chart (bar_facets(), with
# hatching for one series, hatch_segments()), an exact interval for a share
# (share_cp()), and a difference between two shares with its interval and
# test (share_diff()).
# READS / WRITES: nothing.

# GUARD AGAINST A PRINTED NUMBER. The paper prints most values to two or three
# decimals. A printed value v with k decimals is matched when the computed x
# lies within half a unit of the last decimal (0.0005 for three decimals,
# 0.005 for two), that is, when x rounds to v. same() cannot do this job: it
# compares RELATIVE differences, so a small value such as r = .038 would fail
# against its own rounded form. The 1e-12 absorbs floating-point noise at the
# exact half-way point.
paper_same <- function(x, v, digits, what) {
  # all() so that a vector of values (one per grouping, say) is checked
  # element by element against a vector of printed values of the same length.
  stopifnot(length(x) == length(v), length(x) >= 1)
  if (!isTRUE(all(abs(as.numeric(x) - v) <= 0.5 * 10^(-digits) + 1e-12)))
    stop("Guard failed against the paper: ", what, " (computed ", signif(x, 6),
         ", paper ", v, ")")
  invisible(TRUE)
}

# GUARD ON EACH NUMBER SEPARATELY. same() on a vector checks one relative
# difference for the whole vector, so a small entry beside large ones (a d
# of 0.00 beside a t of 7) is barely checked. same_each() runs same() on each
# pair on its own, so every entry must agree to 1e-8 relative to ITS OWN size
# (absolutely, if that size is below 1e-8). The message names the entry.
same_each <- function(a, b, what, labels = seq_along(a), tol = 1e-8) {
  stopifnot(length(a) == length(b), length(a) == length(labels))
  for (i in seq_along(a)) same(a[i], b[i], paste0(what, ", ", labels[i]), tol = tol)
  invisible(TRUE)
}

# GUARD ON A p-VALUE. A p-value can be as small as 1e-80, so neither same()
# (which switches to an ABSOLUTE difference below 1e-8, where any two tiny p's
# agree) nor a fixed absolute tolerance can check it. same_p() demands
# agreement RELATIVE to the target's own size: |a - b| <= rel * |b| + floor.
#   floor = 0 (the default) where both p's come from the same computation, as
#     in the group contrasts: 01 and this document both call t.test().
#   floor = 1e-15 for the dependent correlations. The exports hold cocor's
#     one-sided p, 1 - pnorm(Z), which loses digits to cancellation once p is
#     small (its absolute error is about 2e-16, a relative error of about 5e-6
#     at p = 7.5e-12) and underflows to exactly 0 once Z passes about 8.3.
#     This document's p, pnorm(-Z), has neither fault. The floor absorbs the
#     cancellation and nothing more: a p of 7.5e-12 that was doubled would
#     still fail. Where the export's p is 0, the check reduces to "this p is
#     below 1e-15", and the guard on Z (same_each(), in chk_dep()) is what
#     ties the two together.
same_p <- function(a, b, what, rel = 1e-8, floor = 0) {
  a <- as.numeric(a); b <- as.numeric(b)
  stopifnot(length(a) == length(b), length(a) >= 1, !anyNA(a), !anyNA(b))
  if (!isTRUE(all(abs(a - b) <= rel * abs(b) + floor)))
    stop("Guard failed: ", what, " (", paste(signif(a, 6), collapse = ", "),
         " vs ", paste(signif(b, 6), collapse = ", "), ")")
  invisible(TRUE)
}

# COHEN'S d prints with its leading zero (0.59, not .59), as the paper prints
# it, because d is not bounded by 1; negative values take a true minus sign.
fmt_d <- function(x) sub("^-", "−", sprintf("%.2f", x))
axis_d <- function(x) sub("^-", "−", sprintf("%.1f", x))

# INTERVALS THAT STAY VISIBLE INSIDE A DARK BAR. Every interval is drawn in
# black (INK). On the two darkest bar grays that line all but disappears: black
# on G1 (#1a1a1a) is a contrast of about 1.2 to 1, and on G2 (#404040) about 2
# to 1. The half of the interval that lies inside the bar then vanishes on a
# projector, and the interval seems to start at the end of the bar, so a dark
# bar looks more precise than a light one beside it with the same width of
# interval. (On G3, #737373, black is about 4.4 to 1 and on G4 about 9.7 to 1;
# both read, so those bars keep the plain black interval.)
# THE FIX is a two-tone interval: black where it runs over the white slide,
# white where it runs inside a dark bar. ci_knockout() returns the layers that
# redraw the inside part (and, where there are caps, the lower cap) in white.
# DARK_FILLS names the grays that need it.
DARK_FILLS <- c(G1, G2)
# mark_dark() adds the logical column `dark` the knock-out layers read: TRUE
# where the bar's fill is one of DARK_FILLS.
#   df     the plotted data; fill  the column that picks each bar's gray;
#   fills  the named vector of grays given to scale_fill_manual(); v  the
#   column holding the bar's value (r or d).
mark_dark <- function(df, fill, fills, v) {
  # Every level must have a gray, or the lookup below would give NA and the
  # bar would silently keep an invisible interval.
  stopifnot(all(as.character(df[[fill]]) %in% names(fills)))
  df$dark <- unname(fills[as.character(df[[fill]])]) %in% DARK_FILLS
  # GUARD: the knock-out below assumes every dark bar points to the RIGHT of
  # zero (its inside part runs from max(lower, 0) to the bar's end). That holds
  # for every dark bar in this document (revenge's r and its share agreeing,
  # the blameworthiness d's, and the contrasts at one-sided p < .05 in the
  # registered direction). A
  # negative dark bar would need the mirror-image rule, so the knit stops.
  stopifnot(all(df[[v]][df$dark] > 0))
  df
}
# ci_knockout(): the white layers.
#   v          the column holding the bar's value, as a string ("r" or "d").
#   linewidth  the black interval's own line width, so the white exactly
#              covers it.
#   cap_width  the black interval's cap width; 0 draws no caps.
# The white segment runs from the lower end of the interval, or from zero if
# the interval crosses zero (pmax(lower, 0): the part left of zero lies on the
# white slide and stays black), to the end of the bar. The interval's upper
# end is never inside the bar (the interval always contains the estimate), so
# only the lower cap is redrawn, and only where it lies inside the bar
# (lower > 0).
# DANGER: these layers must be added AFTER the black geom_errorbar(). Layers
# are drawn in the order they are added; placed before it, the white would be
# painted over by the black and the fix would silently do nothing.
ci_knockout <- function(v, linewidth, cap_width = 0) {
  in_bar <- function(k) k[k$dark, , drop = FALSE]
  layers <- list(geom_linerange(data = in_bar,
                                aes(xmin = pmax(lower, 0), xmax = .data[[v]]),
                                orientation = "y", linewidth = linewidth,
                                colour = "white"))
  if (cap_width > 0)
    layers <- c(layers, list(geom_errorbar(
      data = function(k) k[k$dark & k$lower > 0, , drop = FALSE],
      # xmin = xmax = lower: a cap alone, with no horizontal line.
      aes(xmin = lower, xmax = lower), width = cap_width, orientation = "y",
      linewidth = linewidth, colour = "white")))
  layers
}

# HORIZONTAL BAR CHART OF CORRELATIONS WITH THREE-DECIMAL VALUES. bar_r() above
# prints r to two decimals. On slides 2 to 4 that would mislead: revenge
# (.676) and desert theory (.674) would print as .68 and .67, a gap that looks
# real but is .002 (H10, one-sided p = .47). The paper reports these
# correlations to three decimals, so these slides do too. Otherwise identical
# to bar_r() with one bar per row (no dodge), except that a WHITE bar gets a
# black outline (edge_of(), below), so a white bar can mark the one new and
# exploratory score (severity-deserts) on slides 2 and 4.
bar_r3 <- function(df, y, fill, fills, xlim, xbreaks, xlab) {
  df <- mark_dark(df, fill, fills, "r")   # which bars take the white knock-out
  df$edge <- edge_of(df, fill, fills)     # black outline on white bars only
  ggplot(df, aes(x = r, y = .data[[y]], fill = .data[[fill]])) +
    # colour = edge draws the outline; scale_colour_identity() below takes the
    # column's colours as they are ("transparent" = no outline).
    geom_col(aes(colour = edge), width = 0.68, linewidth = 0.9) +
    scale_colour_identity() +
    geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), width = 0.22,
                  orientation = "y", linewidth = 0.7, colour = INK) +
    # The part of the interval inside a dark bar, redrawn in white (see
    # ci_knockout(); DANGER: it must follow the black errorbar layer).
    ci_knockout("r", linewidth = 0.7, cap_width = 0.22) +
    geom_text(aes(x = pmax(upper, 0) + 0.012, label = fmt_r(r, digits = 3)), hjust = 0,
              size = 6, colour = INK, show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = INK2, linewidth = 0.6) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = fills) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = xbreaks, labels = axis_r) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = xlim, clip = "off") +
    labs(x = xlab, y = NULL) +
    theme_hbar()
}

# HORIZONTAL BAR CHART OF COHEN'S d, the counterpart of bar_r() for group
# differences. Same geometry and the same zoom-without-dropping rule; only the
# column (d rather than r) and the number format differ. The value is printed
# past the end of the interval on the side the bar points to.
bar_d <- function(df, y, fill, fills, xlim, xbreaks, xlab) {
  df <- mark_dark(df, fill, fills, "d")   # which bars take the white knock-out
  ggplot(df, aes(x = d, y = .data[[y]], fill = .data[[fill]])) +
    geom_col(width = 0.68) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), width = 0.22,
                  orientation = "y", linewidth = 0.7, colour = INK) +
    # The part of the interval inside a dark bar, redrawn in white (see
    # ci_knockout(); DANGER: it must follow the black errorbar layer).
    ci_knockout("d", linewidth = 0.7, cap_width = 0.22) +
    geom_text(aes(x = ifelse(d >= 0, upper + 0.015, lower - 0.015),
                  hjust = ifelse(d >= 0, 0, 1), label = fmt_d(d)),
              size = 6, colour = INK, show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = INK2, linewidth = 0.6) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = fills) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = xbreaks, labels = axis_d) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = xlim, clip = "off") +
    labs(x = xlab, y = NULL) +
    theme_hbar()
}

# A GROUP CONTRAST EXACTLY AS 01 RUNS IT (welch_contrast(), section 0).
#   y  the outcome; g  a factor whose FIRST level is the retributive side, so
#   a positive d means retributivists (or the retributive side) score higher.
# Welch's t test (unequal variances), a one-sided p from a second run in the
# predicted direction (never a halved two-sided p), and Cohen's d from
# effectsize::cohens_d() with pooled_sd = FALSE: the difference in means over
# the square root of the mean of the two group variances, with its
# noncentral-t 95% interval. Rows missing the outcome or the group are dropped
# for this contrast only, and droplevels() removes an empty level (the middle
# third, which the thirds grouping codes NA).
# DANGER: pooled_sd = FALSE is what 01 uses. The effectsize default (pooled)
# gives a slightly different d, and every guard against the exports would fail.
welch_d <- function(y, g, alternative = "greater") {
  ok <- !is.na(y) & !is.na(g)
  y <- as.numeric(y[ok]); g <- droplevels(factor(g[ok]))
  stopifnot(nlevels(g) == 2)
  lv <- levels(g)
  tmp <- data.frame(y = y, g = g)
  tt <- stats::t.test(y ~ g, data = tmp)                       # level 1 - level 2
  pd <- stats::t.test(y ~ g, data = tmp, alternative = alternative)$p.value
  cd <- effectsize::cohens_d(y ~ g, data = tmp, pooled_sd = FALSE, ci = 0.95)
  data.frame(n1 = sum(g == lv[1]), n2 = sum(g == lv[2]),
             M1 = mean(y[g == lv[1]]), M2 = mean(y[g == lv[2]]),
             t = unname(tt$statistic), df = unname(tt$parameter), p_dir = pd,
             d = cd$Cohens_d, lower = cd$CI_low, upper = cd$CI_high)
}

# A PAIRED COMPARISON EXACTLY AS 01 RUNS IT (paired_test(), section 0), for
# H9-style differences in endorsement: a - b for each participant. The paired
# d is the mean difference divided by the SD of the differences, and its
# interval comes from effectsize::cohens_d(paired = TRUE), as in 01.
# DANGER: this paired d is standardized on the SD of the DIFFERENCES, not of
# the scores. It is not on the same footing as the group d's on slides 5 to 7
# and must not be set beside them as though it were.
paired_diff <- function(a, b, alternative = "greater") {
  ok <- stats::complete.cases(a, b)
  a <- as.numeric(a[ok]); b <- as.numeric(b[ok])
  tt <- stats::t.test(a, b, paired = TRUE)
  pd <- stats::t.test(a, b, paired = TRUE, alternative = alternative)$p.value
  cd <- effectsize::cohens_d(a, b, paired = TRUE, ci = 0.95)
  data.frame(n = length(a), M1 = mean(a), M2 = mean(b), mean_diff = mean(a - b),
             diff_lower = tt$conf.int[1], diff_upper = tt$conf.int[2],
             t = unname(tt$statistic), df = unname(tt$parameter),
             p_two = tt$p.value, p_one = pd,
             d = mean(a - b) / stats::sd(a - b), d_lower = cd$CI_low,
             d_upper = cd$CI_high)
}

# TWO DEPENDENT, OVERLAPPING CORRELATIONS, as 01's steiger_overlap(): does k
# (revenge) correlate more strongly with j (punitiveness) than h (a rival
# score) does? Both r's come from the same people and share j, so they are
# compared with Steiger's (1980) Z, and the difference r_jk - r_jh gets Zou's
# (2007) interval, both from cocor. complete.cases() across all three columns,
# because the test describes one covariance matrix from one set of people.
# THE p-VALUES are computed here from Z rather than taken from cocor. cocor
# returns 1 - pnorm(Z), which underflows to exactly 0 once Z passes about 8.3
# (revenge against just deserts gives Z = 8.70), and a table that prints p = 0
# states something no test can show. pnorm(-Z) is the same quantity without
# the underflow: 2 * pnorm(-|Z|) two-sided, and pnorm(-Z) one-sided in H10's
# registered direction (revenge higher, so a positive Z). Where cocor's p has
# not underflowed, the two agree to rounding, and the guard below checks that.
# Zou's interval does not depend on the direction of the test.
dep_cor <- function(j, k, h) {
  ok <- stats::complete.cases(j, k, h)
  j <- j[ok]; k <- k[ok]; h <- h[ok]; n <- sum(ok)
  r_jk <- stats::cor(j, k); r_jh <- stats::cor(j, h); r_kh <- stats::cor(k, h)
  cc <- cocor::cocor.dep.groups.overlap(r.jk = r_jk, r.jh = r_jh, r.kh = r_kh, n = n,
                                        alternative = "two.sided",
                                        test = c("steiger1980", "zou2007"))
  z <- unname(cc@steiger1980$statistic)
  p_two <- 2 * stats::pnorm(-abs(z))
  # GUARD: the same two-sided p as cocor's, wherever cocor's is not 0.
  stopifnot(abs(p_two - cc@steiger1980$p.value) < 1e-12)
  data.frame(n = n, r_revenge = r_jk, r_rival = r_jh, r_revenge_rival = r_kh,
             diff = r_jk - r_jh, diff_lower = cc@zou2007$conf.int[1],
             diff_upper = cc@zou2007$conf.int[2],
             z = z, p_two = p_two, p_one = stats::pnorm(-z))
}

# ---- Tools for slides 8 to 11 (and the white bars of slides 2 and 4) --------

# OUTLINES FOR WHITE BARS. Severity-deserts, the one new and exploratory
# score, is marked by a WHITE bar wherever it is a bar. A white bar on a white slide
# has no edge of its own, so it gets a black (INK) outline; every other bar
# gets "transparent", which draws no outline at all. Returns one colour per
# row of df, for scale_colour_identity().
#   df, fill, fills  as in mark_dark(): the data, the column that picks each
#                    bar's gray, and the named vector of grays.
edge_of <- function(df, fill, fills) {
  # Every level must have a gray, or the lookup would give NA (no outline, and
  # a white bar would vanish).
  stopifnot(all(as.character(df[[fill]]) %in% names(fills)))
  ifelse(unname(fills[as.character(df[[fill]])]) == "white", INK, "transparent")
}

# HATCHING FOR ONE SERIES (slide 11's three-item revenge). ggplot2 has no
# pattern fill, so the stripes are drawn as short diagonal line segments
# clipped to the inside of each bar. The bar they sit on is white with a black
# outline, so the series reads as "revenge, a variant": the same ink as
# four-item revenge's solid black bar, but clearly not the same bar, which the
# next-darkest gray (G2, #404040, beside G1's #1a1a1a) would not be on a
# projector.
#   h     the rows to hatch, with columns panel, label (a factor: its level
#         number is the row's position on the discrete y axis), value (the
#         bar's end; must be positive).
#   run   how far, in x units, a stripe travels from the bar's bottom edge to
#         its top edge (sets the stripes' slant).
#   gap   the distance, in x units, between stripes.
#   half  half the bar's thickness in y units: 0.34 for the 0.68-wide bars
#         bar_facets() draws. DANGER: change both together, or the stripes
#         will spill above and below the bar.
# Each stripe starts where x = a on the bar's bottom edge and ends at x = a +
# run on its top edge; the ends are then pulled in to the bar (0 <= x <=
# value), and y is moved along the stripe by the same fraction, so a clipped
# stripe keeps its slant.
hatch_segments <- function(h, run, gap, half = 0.34) {
  stopifnot(is.factor(h$label), all(h$value > 0))
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(h)), function(i) {
    v  <- h$value[i]
    y0 <- as.integer(h$label[i]) - half; y1 <- y0 + 2 * half
    a  <- seq(-run, v, by = gap)                 # where each stripe meets the bottom
    xs <- pmax(a, 0);       ys <- y0 + (xs - a) / run * (y1 - y0)
    xe <- pmin(a + run, v); ye <- y0 + (xe - a) / run * (y1 - y0)
    keep <- xe > xs                               # drop stripes wholly outside the bar
    data.frame(panel = h$panel[i], x = xs[keep], xend = xe[keep],
               y = ys[keep], yend = ye[keep])
  }))
}

# FACETED HORIZONTAL BAR CHART, for slides 8, 9 and 11: the same rows in two or
# three panels side by side. One bar per row per panel, its 95% interval, and
# its value printed past the end of the interval.
#   df      one row per bar, with columns panel (factor, the panel order),
#           label (factor, the row order, bottom to top), value, lower, upper,
#           shade (picks the gray), txt (the printed value, already formatted)
#           and tx (where the printed value starts, in the panel's own units:
#           the interval's end plus a small offset).
#   fills   named vector of grays for the shade levels; "white" gets an outline.
#   lims    a data frame with column x (and panel, where the panels' axes
#           differ): values the axis must reach. Drawn with geom_blank(), which
#           draws nothing but stretches each panel's axis to cover them.
#   breaks, labels   the axis breaks and their labels, as vectors or as
#           functions (functions when the panels' axes differ, slide 8).
#   scales  "fixed" (one shared axis) or "free_x" (each panel its own axis).
#   hatch   the shade levels to hatch (hatch_segments()), or NULL.
# The axis runs exactly to the extremes of the data and lims (no padding), so
# the bars start at the zero line; clip = "off" lets a printed value run past
# the panel's right edge into the space between panels rather than be cut.
bar_facets <- function(df, fills, lims, breaks, labels, xlab, scales = "fixed",
                       hatch = NULL, hatch_run = 0.2, hatch_gap = 0.03) {
  df <- mark_dark(df, "shade", fills, "value")   # which bars take the knock-out
  df$edge <- edge_of(df, "shade", fills)         # outline for white bars
  p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = value, y = label)) +
    # The fills first, without outlines ...
    geom_col(aes(fill = shade), width = 0.68)
  if (!is.null(hatch))
    # ... then any hatching, in G2, thin, so that the black interval drawn
    # over it (thicker, and horizontal) stays the line the eye follows ...
    p <- p + geom_segment(data = hatch_segments(df[df$shade %in% hatch, ],
                                                hatch_run, hatch_gap),
                          aes(x = x, xend = xend, y = y, yend = yend),
                          inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = G2, linewidth = 0.45)
  p +
    # ... then the outlines on top, so no stripe end pokes over an edge.
    geom_col(aes(colour = edge), fill = NA, width = 0.68, linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), width = 0.22,
                  orientation = "y", linewidth = 0.7, colour = INK) +
    # The part of the interval inside a dark bar, redrawn in white (see
    # ci_knockout(); DANGER: it must follow the black errorbar layer).
    ci_knockout("value", linewidth = 0.7, cap_width = 0.22) +
    # THE PRINTED VALUE starts with a space, a gap of about 5 points at this
    # 17-pt size, whatever the panel's width. tx alone is an offset in data
    # units, which shrinks on a narrow panel until the number touches the
    # interval's cap, and a cap beside ".676" reads as a leading 1 ("|.676").
    # DANGER: drop the space and the labels touch their caps on slides 8, 9
    # and 11.
    geom_text(aes(x = tx, label = paste0(" ", txt)), hjust = 0, size = 6, colour = INK) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = INK2, linewidth = 0.6) +
    geom_blank(data = lims, aes(x = x), inherit.aes = FALSE) +
    facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1, scales = scales) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = fills, guide = "none") +
    scale_colour_identity() +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = breaks, labels = labels, expand = expansion(0)) +
    coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
    labs(x = xlab, y = NULL) +
    theme_hbar() +
    theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold", colour = INK,
                                     margin = margin(b = 10)),
          strip.clip = "off")
}

# A SHARE WITH ITS EXACT 95% INTERVAL. The share is the proportion of x that
# is TRUE; the interval is Clopper and Pearson's exact binomial interval, from
# binom.test(), the interval the paper's shares use (H4_shares and the H12
# exports hold exactly these intervals, and the guards on slides 8 and 10
# check that).
share_cp <- function(x) {
  stopifnot(is.logical(x), !anyNA(x))
  k <- sum(x); n <- length(x); ci <- stats::binom.test(k, n)$conf.int
  data.frame(k = k, n = n, share = k / n, lower = ci[1], upper = ci[2])
}

# THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN TWO INDEPENDENT SHARES, k1/n1 - k2/n2, with
#   - its 95% interval by Newcombe's (1998) hybrid score method (his method 10):
#     each share's Wilson score interval, combined as below. It keeps close to
#     95% coverage at these sample sizes and never runs past -1 or 1, which the
#     simple Wald interval (prop.test()'s own interval) can;
#   - its two-sided p from the two-sample test of equal proportions WITHOUT the
#     continuity correction, prop.test(correct = FALSE): the Pearson chi-square
#     on the 2 x 2 table, identical to the pooled two-proportion z test.
# The two come from related but different methods (the p from the pooled z,
# the interval from Wilson scores), as is usual for this difference; the
# values table says which is which.
# Each share's Wilson interval is taken from prop.test(correct = FALSE) on that
# share alone, and a guard checks it against the Wilson formula, so the
# interval cannot silently change meaning if prop.test() ever changes.
share_diff <- function(k1, n1, k2, n2) {
  wilson <- function(k, n, z = stats::qnorm(0.975)) {
    p <- k / n
    (p + z^2 / (2 * n) + c(-1, 1) * z * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z^2 / (4 * n^2))) /
      (1 + z^2 / n)
  }
  w1 <- stats::prop.test(k1, n1, correct = FALSE)$conf.int
  w2 <- stats::prop.test(k2, n2, correct = FALSE)$conf.int
  same_each(c(w1, w2), c(wilson(k1, n1), wilson(k2, n2)), "Wilson interval",
            labels = c("group 1 lower", "group 1 upper", "group 2 lower", "group 2 upper"))
  p1 <- k1 / n1; p2 <- k2 / n2; dlt <- p1 - p2
  # Newcombe's hybrid: the lower end borrows group 1's lower and group 2's
  # upper Wilson distances; the upper end the reverse.
  lo <- dlt - sqrt((p1 - w1[1])^2 + (w2[2] - p2)^2)
  hi <- dlt + sqrt((w1[2] - p1)^2 + (p2 - w2[1])^2)
  pt <- stats::prop.test(c(k1, k2), c(n1, n2), correct = FALSE)
  # GUARD: prop.test()'s p is the pooled two-proportion z test's p.
  pbar <- (k1 + k2) / (n1 + n2)
  z <- dlt / sqrt(pbar * (1 - pbar) * (1 / n1 + 1 / n2))
  same_p(pt$p.value, 2 * stats::pnorm(-abs(z)), "two-proportion test p")
  data.frame(diff = dlt, lower = lo, upper = hi, z = z, p_two = pt$p.value)
}
```

# 3. The scores

```{r scores}
# === THE SCORES EVERY SLIDE USES ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: assembles, in one data frame `sc`, one row per
# participant with punitiveness, revenge, desert theory, the proportionality
# principle, just deserts, the severity index, and the new severity-deserts
# score, plus the retributivist flag and the grouping the main text uses
# (retributivists against the deterrence- or incapacitation-first). Guards tie
# each score to its items and to the paper's exports.
# READS: d (the scored data) and PAPER_person_scores (the paper's scores,
#        written by 01, sections 9.19A and 9.19G).
# MATCHES: Method, Study 2 ("Punitiveness", "Revenge and proportionality",
#          "Goals of punishment"); Results, Part 2.
#
# DANGER: THE SCORED DATA CARRY THE REGISTERED SCORES UNDER THE OBVIOUS NAMES.
# In retribution_scored.rds, `punitiveness` is the eight-item scale, `deserved`
# is the registered four-item desert score, and `just_deserts` is the
# registered just deserts (the four desert items with the three-item
# proportionality component). NONE of these is what the paper reports. The
# paper's punitiveness, desert theory and just deserts are in
# PAPER_person_scores and are taken from there. Reading d$just_deserts where
# the paper's score is meant would put a mean of 5.38 on the slide instead of
# 5.66 and move every correlation.
ps <- read_s2("PAPER_person_scores")
# The export is keyed by ResponseId and written in the order of `d`; if the
# order ever differed, every score would land on the wrong participant, so
# the order is checked, not assumed.
stopifnot(identical(ps$ResponseId, d$ResponseId), !anyNA(ps))

sc <- data.frame(ResponseId = d$ResponseId, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
# PUNITIVENESS (the paper's): the six components (support for more punishment,
# rejection of parsimony, three-strikes laws, life without parole, the death
# penalty, and the first sentence standardized within vignette), each
# standardized across the sample and then averaged, so each carries a sixth
# of the weight.
sc$punit <- ps$punit_six
# REVENGE: the four registered items, averaged. The fourth ("Rather than
# showing criminals so much tolerance, we should be punishing them more
# severely") is kept, as in the paper. Revenge on Study 1's three items
# (revenge_1 to _3, without the harsher-punishment item) is built for the
# check rows of the tests table and for slide 11, the backup; no main-line
# slide shows it.
sc$revenge  <- d$revenge
sc$revenge3 <- rowMeans(d[, paste0("revenge_", 1:3)])
# DESERT THEORY: the mean of the five desert items, Retribution_1 to _5.
sc$desert_theory <- ps$desert_theory
# THE PROPORTIONALITY PRINCIPLE: the single item "Punishment should be
# proportionate to the severity of the crime, no more and no less" (1 to 7).
sc$proportionality_principle <- d$proportionality_principle
# JUST DESERTS (the paper's): the mean of desert theory and the principle.
sc$just_deserts <- ps$just_deserts
# THE SEVERITY INDEX: the mean of "Punishment should be greater than the
# seriousness of the crime" (severity_1) and "Punishment should be less severe
# than the harmfulness of the crime" (severity_2) REVERSED, so that a high
# score means punishment at or above the offense and never below it.
sc$severity_index <- d$severity_index
# SEVERITY-DESERTS (NEW, Dan's proposal; NOT PREREGISTERED; exploratory): the
# mean of desert theory and the severity index. It is built exactly as just
# deserts is built, a plain mean of two 1-to-7 scores, so the two composites
# differ only in their second part (the principle against the index).
# DANGER: do not standardize the two parts before averaging. Just deserts
# averages its raw parts, and severity-deserts must be built the same way, or
# the comparison between the two composites would mix two scoring rules.
sc$severity_deserts <- (sc$desert_theory + sc$severity_index) / 2
sc$retributivist <- d$retributivist

# GUARDS: EACH SCORE IS WHAT ITS NAME SAYS.
#   1. Desert theory is the mean of Retribution_1 to _5.
#   2. The principle is the raw item as answered.
#   3. Just deserts is (desert theory + principle) / 2, the identity the Method
#      states.
#   4. The severity index is (severity_1 + (8 - severity_2)) / 2; the reverse of
#      a 1-to-7 item is 8 minus the answer, and severity_2_R must be exactly
#      that reverse.
#   5. Revenge is the mean of its four items.
#   6. No score is missing: every rating item required an answer.
same(sc$desert_theory, rowMeans(d[, paste0("Retribution_", 1:5)]), "desert theory = mean of items 1-5")
same(sc$proportionality_principle, d$proportionality, "principle = the raw item")
same(sc$just_deserts, (sc$desert_theory + sc$proportionality_principle) / 2,
     "just deserts = (desert theory + principle) / 2")
same(d$severity_2_R, 8 - d$severity_2, "severity_2 reversed = 8 - severity_2")
same(sc$severity_index, (d$severity_1 + (8 - d$severity_2)) / 2,
     "severity index = mean of severity_1 and severity_2 reversed")
same(sc$revenge, rowMeans(d[, paste0("revenge_", 1:4)]), "revenge = mean of its four items")
stopifnot(!anyNA(sc))

# WHO RANKED WHAT FIRST, rebuilt with 01's rule (9.12b, cq_first).
# Prioritization_1 to _4 hold the ranks given to the four reasons in the
# instrument's order: 1 retribution ("Criminals deserve to be punished"),
# 2 deterrence, 3 incapacitation, 4 rehabilitation. The goal ranked first is
# the column holding the 1. A row with a missing rank or no 1 would be unknown
# (NA), never credited to a goal; there are none.
# DANGER: the column ORDER stands in for the goal's name, as it does in 01.
# Reordering prio_cols would silently relabel the goals; the guard on the
# retributivists below catches a change that moves retribution, and the guard
# on the four counts catches any other.
prio_cols <- paste0("Prioritization_", 1:4)
first <- apply(d[, prio_cols], 1, function(r) {
  if (anyNA(r) || !any(r == 1)) return(NA_integer_)
  which(r == 1)[1]
})
stopifnot(!anyNA(first),
          identical(which(first == 1), which(d$retributivist == 1)),
          identical(as.integer(table(factor(first, levels = 1:4))),
                    c(371L, 187L, 266L, 124L)))   # Part 3: 371, 187, 266, 124
# THE MAIN TEXT'S COMPARISON: retributivists (first level, so a positive d
# means retributivists higher) against those who ranked deterrence or
# incapacitation first. Those who ranked rehabilitation first are NA, and
# welch_d() drops them, as 01's welch_contrast() does.
sc$grp_vs_deter_incap <- factor(
  ifelse(first == 1, "Retributivist",
         ifelse(first %in% c(2, 3), "Deterrence or incapacitation first", NA_character_)),
  levels = c("Retributivist", "Deterrence or incapacitation first"))
stopifnot(identical(as.integer(table(sc$grp_vs_deter_incap)), c(371L, 453L)))

# THE FOUR REGISTERED GROUPINGS, as the scored data carry them. Each factor's
# first level is the retributive side (01, Phase 5), and the counts are the
# ones the paper reports (Part 3 and Table S16).
for (g in c("grp_rank", "grp_med", "grp_tert", "grp_ratio")) sc[[g]] <- d[[g]]
stopifnot(identical(as.integer(table(droplevels(sc$grp_rank))),  c(371L, 577L)),
          identical(as.integer(table(droplevels(sc$grp_med))),   c(470L, 478L)),
          identical(as.integer(table(droplevels(sc$grp_tert))),  c(314L, 317L)),
          identical(as.integer(table(droplevels(sc$grp_ratio))), c(514L, 433L)),
          levels(sc$grp_rank)[1] == "Retributivist")

# GUARDS AGAINST THE EXPORTS. The means of the paper's scores are the ones the
# H9 exports hold (the paper's scorings, whole sample), and the parts of just
# deserts have the means PAPER_JD_parts holds.
h9 <- read_s2("PAPER_H9"); jd9 <- read_s2("PAPER_JD_H9"); jdp <- read_s2("PAPER_JD_parts")
same(mean(sc$desert_theory), h9$M1, "desert theory mean (PAPER_H9)")
same(mean(sc$revenge),       h9$M2, "revenge mean (PAPER_H9)")
same(mean(sc$just_deserts),  jd9$M1[jd9$var1 == "just_deserts"], "just deserts mean (PAPER_JD_H9)")
same(mean(sc$proportionality_principle), jdp$M_principle[jdp$sample == "Whole sample"],
     "principle mean (PAPER_JD_parts)")
cat(sprintf("Means: revenge %.2f, desert theory %.2f, just deserts %.2f, severity index %.2f, severity-deserts %.2f\n",
            mean(sc$revenge), mean(sc$desert_theory), mean(sc$just_deserts),
            mean(sc$severity_index), mean(sc$severity_deserts)))

# THE FOUR SCORES the first four slides compare, in the order they take on
# every slide: revenge first, then desert theory, then the two composites.
SCORES <- c(revenge = "Revenge", desert_theory = "Desert theory",
            just_deserts = "Just deserts", severity_deserts = "Severity-deserts")
# Shading on the bar charts (slides 2, 4 and 9): revenge in the darkest gray;
# desert theory and just deserts in the mid gray G3; severity-deserts WHITE
# with a black outline (bar_r3() and bar_facets() outline every white bar), so
# the one new and exploratory score stands apart from the paper's scores, and
# every caption can point to "the white bar". Every bar is also named on its
# axis, so no legend is needed.
# WHY G3 AND NOT THE LIGHTEST GRAY (G4, #b0b0b0) for the desert bars: G4
# washes out to near-white on a projector, which would make
# desert theory, the bar that ties revenge, look fainter than it is. On G3 a
# black interval is still about 4.4 to 1, so those bars keep plain black
# intervals; only G1 takes the white knock-out (mark_dark()).
FAMILY <- c(revenge = "Revenge", desert_theory = "Desert", just_deserts = "Desert",
            severity_deserts = "Exploratory")
FAMILY_FILLS <- c(Revenge = G1, Desert = G3, Exploratory = "white")
```

# 4. Revenge, desert theory, just deserts, and severity-deserts

```{r fig01_endorsement, fig.width = 13.333, fig.height = 7.5}
# === SLIDE 1: HOW MUCH PARTICIPANTS ENDORSED EACH SCORE (VIOLIN PLOT) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: one violin per score (revenge, desert theory, just
# deserts, severity-deserts), each on its 1-to-7 scale, with every participant
# as a point and the mean with its 95% interval.
# READS: sc (section 3); PAPER_H9 and PAPER_JD_H9 for the guards.
# WRITES: pt_01_endorsement (PNG, PDF, Docs copy); its values.
# MATCHES: Results, Part 2, H9 ("M = 5.60 against 4.14"; just deserts
#          M = 5.66). Severity-deserts is new and not in the paper.
#
# The x labels carry each score's make-up, so the caption can be kept to the
# wording of the two parts the composites add. A composite is labelled by its
# two parts joined with "and" ("desert theory and proportionality"), never with
# a "+", which would read as a sum; the Method defines each as the MEAN of its
# two parts.
# THE COMPOSITES' LABELS name both parts in the paper's terms. Just deserts is
# "desert theory and proportionality principle", never "... and
# proportionality" alone: the Supplement also reports a three-item
# "proportionality component", the one in the registered just-deserts score,
# and the short form would leave open which of the two this composite uses.
# Severity-deserts, the one new and exploratory score, says so on its label
# ("new, exploratory"), so the violin cannot be read as one of the paper's
# scores. Both composite labels take four lines; the axis is as tall as its
# tallest label, so the two cost no more height than one would.
# LINE BREAKS. The violins sit about 2.4 inches apart, and at 17 pt no line of
# a label may be much wider than 2 inches or it runs into its neighbour (a
# line such as "(mean of desert theory", 2.4 inches, would touch the next
# label). The widest line here, "(desert theory and", is about 1.9 inches.
SCORE_X <- c(revenge = "Revenge\n(four items)",
             desert_theory = "Desert theory\n(five items)",
             just_deserts = "Just deserts\n(desert theory and\nproportionality\nprinciple)",
             severity_deserts = "Severity-deserts\n(desert theory and\nseverity index;\nnew, exploratory)")
endorse <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(SCORES), function(v)
  cbind(measure = SCORE_X[[v]], key = v, mean_ci(sc[[v]]))))
# GUARDS: the three means the paper reports, against the exports (1e-8) and
# against the printed two-decimal values.
same(endorse$mean[endorse$key == "revenge"],       h9$M2, "slide 1: revenge mean")
same(endorse$mean[endorse$key == "desert_theory"], h9$M1, "slide 1: desert theory mean")
same(endorse$mean[endorse$key == "just_deserts"],
     jd9$M1[jd9$var1 == "just_deserts"], "slide 1: just deserts mean")
paper_same(endorse$mean[endorse$key == "revenge"],       4.14, 2, "revenge mean 4.14")
paper_same(endorse$mean[endorse$key == "desert_theory"], 5.60, 2, "desert theory mean 5.60")
paper_same(endorse$mean[endorse$key == "just_deserts"],  5.66, 2, "just deserts mean 5.66")
stopifnot(all(endorse$n == 948))

endorse_long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(SCORES), function(v)
  data.frame(measure = SCORE_X[[v]], score = sc[[v]])))
fig01 <- violin_1to7(endorse_long, endorse, unname(SCORE_X)) +
  # THE SEVERITY INDEX GLOSS is the Method's own sentence ("a high score means
  # punishment at or above the offense and never below it"). DANGER: do not
  # paraphrase it as "punishment greater than the crime"; the index's high end
  # is punishment AT or above the offense, not only above it.
  labs(title = "Endorsing Revenge and Desert",
       caption = cap("N = 948. Proportionality principle: “Punishment should be proportionate to the severity of the crime, no more and no less.”",
                     "Severity index: a high score means punishment at or above the offense and never below it. Black points: means with 95% CIs.")) +
  # The two- to four-line x labels need a little less line spacing to sit
  # compactly under their violins; 17 pt keeps the longest line inside its
  # own column (see LINE BREAKS above).
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(colour = INK, size = 17, lineheight = 0.92))
save_slide(fig01, "pt_01_endorsement")
keep_values("pt_01_endorsement", data.frame(
  label = paste("Mean (1 to 7):", SCORES[endorse$key]), value = endorse$mean,
  lower = endorse$lower, upper = endorse$upper, n = endorse$n))
fig01
```

```{r fig02_punitiveness, fig.width = 13.333, fig.height = 7.5}
# === SLIDE 2: HOW CLOSELY EACH SCORE TRACKS PUNITIVENESS, WHOLE SAMPLE ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: the correlation of each of the four scores with
# punitiveness (the paper's six-component score), with its Fisher 95%
# interval, as horizontal bars.
# READS: sc; PAPER_H10_cors and PAPER_JD_H10_cors for the guards.
# WRITES: pt_02_punitiveness; its values.
# MATCHES: Results, Part 2, H10: revenge r = .676 [.640, .709], desert theory
#          .674 [.638, .708], just deserts .432 [.379, .482]. Severity-deserts
#          (.734) is new; it is guarded against its value computed
#          independently of this document.
# A backup slide: slide 9, in the main line, shows these four correlations
# beside slide 4's, reusing `assoc` and its guards. The desert bars are mid
# gray (G3), severity-deserts is a white bar with a black outline, and the
# caption marks it as new and exploratory.
assoc <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(SCORES), function(v)
  cbind(label = SCORES[[v]], key = v, family = FAMILY[[v]], cor_ci(sc$punit, sc[[v]]))))
# GUARDS: each r and both ends of its interval against the export row that
# holds it (1e-8), then against the paper's three-decimal values.
h10c <- read_s2("PAPER_H10_cors"); jd10c <- read_s2("PAPER_JD_H10_cors")
pick_cor <- function(tab, sample, y, x = "Punitiveness (six components)")
  tab[tab$sample == sample & tab$x == x & tab$y == y, ]
chk2 <- list(revenge = pick_cor(h10c, "Whole sample", "Revenge"),
             desert_theory = pick_cor(h10c, "Whole sample", "Desert theory"),
             just_deserts = pick_cor(jd10c, "Whole sample", "Just deserts"))
for (v in names(chk2)) {
  stopifnot(nrow(chk2[[v]]) == 1)
  a <- assoc[assoc$key == v, ]
  same(c(a$r, a$lower, a$upper), c(chk2[[v]]$r, chk2[[v]]$ci_lower, chk2[[v]]$ci_upper),
       paste("slide 2: r and CI,", v))
}
paper_same(assoc$r[assoc$key == "revenge"],          .676, 3, "r(punitiveness, revenge) .676")
paper_same(assoc$r[assoc$key == "desert_theory"],    .674, 3, "r(punitiveness, desert theory) .674")
paper_same(assoc$r[assoc$key == "just_deserts"],     .432, 3, "r(punitiveness, just deserts) .432")
paper_same(assoc$r[assoc$key == "severity_deserts"], .734, 3, "r(punitiveness, severity-deserts) .734 (new; computed independently)")
stopifnot(all(assoc$n == 948))

# Revenge on top: rows are drawn bottom-up, so the levels are reversed.
assoc$label <- factor(assoc$label, levels = rev(unname(SCORES)))
fig02 <- bar_r3(assoc, "label", "family", fills = FAMILY_FILLS,
               xlim = c(0, 0.84), xbreaks = seq(0, 0.8, 0.2),
               xlab = "Correlation with punitiveness (r)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  # REGISTRATION WORDING. The caption says severity-deserts is "new and
  # exploratory", not that it "was not preregistered": that
  # wording would imply that the other three bars were, and they were not as
  # scored here (desert theory and the paper's just deserts both depart from
  # the preregistration; Method, Analytic Strategy). "New" says it is not in
  # the paper; "exploratory" says that no hypothesis, registered or rerun,
  # bears on it. The registered tests are in the Supplement (Section S4).
  # "(white bar)" ties the words to the bar: severity-deserts is the only
  # white bar (FAMILY_FILLS, section 3).
  # THE CAPTION, one sentence group per line, so neither line breaks inside a
  # sentence or a list. Punitiveness is defined in the same words as on
  # slides 8 and 9: "two punitive attitudes" are support for more punishment
  # and rejection of parsimony; "three policies" are three-strikes laws, life
  # without parole and the death penalty. The six listed one by one do not
  # fit on one line, and a list split across two lines is hard to take in.
  labs(title = "Revenge, Desert, and Punitiveness",
       caption = cap("N = 948. Punitiveness: six standardized components (two punitive attitudes, three policies, the first sentence).",
                     "Error bars: 95% CIs. Severity-deserts (white bar) is new and exploratory."))
save_slide(fig02, "pt_02_punitiveness")
keep_values("pt_02_punitiveness", data.frame(
  label = paste("r with punitiveness, whole sample:", assoc$label), value = assoc$r,
  lower = assoc$lower, upper = assoc$upper, n = assoc$n))
fig02
```

```{r fig03_parts, fig.width = 13.333, fig.height = 7.5}
# === SLIDE 3: THE PARTS OF THE TWO COMPOSITES, EACH WITH PUNITIVENESS ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: the correlation with punitiveness of desert theory
# (the part both composites share), the proportionality principle (the second
# part of just deserts) and the severity index (the second part of
# severity-deserts). A composite that averages two parts goes with
# punitiveness roughly in proportion to what its parts bring, so this slide
# shows where the two composites' correlations on slide 2 come from.
# READS: sc; PAPER_H10_cors and PAPER_H6 for the guards.
# WRITES: pt_03_parts; its values.
# MATCHES: Results, Part 2, H6 ("r = .588 with the severity index against .038
#          with the principle"; not registered) and H10 (desert theory .674).
PARTS <- c(desert_theory = "Desert theory\n(in both composites)",
           proportionality_principle = "Proportionality principle\n(in just deserts)",
           severity_index = "Severity index\n(in severity-deserts)")
parts <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(PARTS), function(v)
  cbind(label = PARTS[[v]], key = v, cor_ci(sc$punit, sc[[v]]))))
# GUARDS: desert theory against PAPER_H10_cors; the principle and the index
# against the H6 comparison for punitiveness (PAPER_H6: r_jk is the index,
# r_jh the principle); then against the paper's printed values.
h6 <- read_s2("PAPER_H6"); h6p <- h6[h6$pair == "Punitiveness (six components)", ]
stopifnot(nrow(h6p) == 1)
same(parts$r[parts$key == "desert_theory"], chk2$desert_theory$r, "slide 3: desert theory r")
same(parts$r[parts$key == "severity_index"], h6p$r_jk, "slide 3: severity index r (PAPER_H6)")
same(parts$r[parts$key == "proportionality_principle"], h6p$r_jh, "slide 3: principle r (PAPER_H6)")
paper_same(parts$r[parts$key == "severity_index"], .588, 3, "r(punitiveness, severity index) .588")
paper_same(parts$r[parts$key == "proportionality_principle"], .038, 3,
           "r(punitiveness, principle) .038")
stopifnot(all(parts$n == 948))

parts$label <- factor(parts$label, levels = rev(unname(PARTS)))
# One gray for all three bars: the slide compares three parts, not families.
parts$shade <- "part"
fig03 <- bar_r3(parts, "label", "shade", fills = c(part = G3),
               xlim = c(-0.08, 0.8), xbreaks = seq(0, 0.8, 0.2),
               xlab = "Correlation with punitiveness (r)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        axis.text.y = element_text(colour = INK, size = 19, lineheight = 0.95)) +
  # THE CAPTION: N, the intervals, the two items of the severity index (the
  # second reverse-scored) and that none of the three correlations was
  # preregistered. The two items together are too long for one line, so the
  # line breaks between them, never inside a quoted item: each item is read
  # whole, as the participants read it. "Error bars" is on the first line to
  # keep the second as short as the other slides' lines.
  labs(title = "The Parts and Punitiveness",
       caption = cap("N = 948. Error bars: 95% CIs. Severity index: “Punishment should be greater than the seriousness of the crime” and, reversed,",
                     "“Punishment should be less severe than the harmfulness of the crime.” None of these correlations was preregistered."))
save_slide(fig03, "pt_03_parts")
keep_values("pt_03_parts", data.frame(
  label = paste("r with punitiveness, whole sample:", gsub("\n.*", "", parts$label)),
  value = parts$r, lower = parts$lower, upper = parts$upper, n = parts$n))
fig03
```

```{r tests}
# === THE TESTS BEHIND SLIDES 1 TO 4 (TABLE, NOT DRAWN) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: two families of tests, written to
# princeton_talk_tests.csv.
#   A. WHICH SCORE GOES MORE CLOSELY WITH PUNITIVENESS. Revenge against desert
#      theory, just deserts and severity-deserts, in the whole sample and
#      among retributivists, each by Steiger's Z with Zou's interval for the
#      difference in r. Revenge is scored with its four registered items and,
#      as a check, with Study 1's three items.
#   B. WHICH SCORE PARTICIPANTS ENDORSED MORE (H9-style). Each desert-based
#      score minus revenge, participant by participant: the mean difference,
#      its 95% interval, the paired t, and the paired d as 01 computes it. The
#      difference is taken as the desert score minus revenge so that its sign
#      matches the paper's (1.46, d = 1.18, for desert theory).
# READS: sc; the H9, H10 and H11 exports for the guards.
# WRITES: nothing yet; slide 11 (section 7) adds six rows and an `outcome`
#         column, and the table is written in section 8.
# MATCHES: Results, Part 2 (H9, H10) and Part 3 (H11); Table S17.
#
# WHAT IS REGISTERED, AND WHAT THIS TABLE HOLDS. H10 registered a comparison
# of revenge with just deserts, one-sided (revenge goes more closely with
# punitiveness); H9 registered just deserts against revenge, one-sided (just
# deserts endorsed more); H11 repeats both among retributivists. The
# REGISTERED TESTS are run on the registered just-deserts score (the
# registered desert items 1 to 4 averaged with the three-item proportionality
# component) and are in the Supplement: Table S12 for H9 and H10 (H9: d = 0.90;
# H10: delta r = .251, Z = 8.96, on the eight-item scale), Table S17 for H11
# (delta r = .384; H9's d = 0.76). NONE OF THOSE ROWS IS IN THIS TABLE.
# This table uses the paper's scorings, and neither was registered:
#   - just deserts as the mean of desert theory and the proportionality
#     principle ("Scoring the two parts as one departs from the
#     preregistration", Analytic Strategy; Supplement: "That score was not
#     registered"). These rows rerun the registered hypothesis, in its
#     registered direction, on that score.
#   - desert theory, the five desert-theory items, which the paper reports
#     beside just deserts; also a rerun in the registered direction.
# A rerun of a registered one-sided test on another scoring keeps the
# registered direction (Analytic Strategy; Supplement S4), so these rows carry
# a one-sided p. Three-item revenge rows are rescorings of revenge, so they
# too keep the registered direction.
# Severity-deserts is a new score, not a rescoring of just deserts (it has no
# proportionality in it), so its rows rerun no registered test: they are
# exploratory and two-sided only, and their one-sided p is left blank.
# DANGER: never label a row here "registered test". The registered test is
# on the registered just-deserts score and gives different numbers; quoting
# .244 / Z = 8.70 or d = 1.08 as "the registered test" would misstate it.
RIVALS <- c(desert_theory = "Desert theory", just_deserts = "Just deserts",
            severity_deserts = "Severity-deserts")
# Three-item revenge is named by its source, Study 1's three items: the
# Supplement reports two three-item scorings (Table S12: without the father
# item, and Study 1's three items, which leave out the harsher-punishment
# item), and "three items" alone would not say which.
REV_SCORING <- c(revenge = "Revenge, four items",
                 revenge3 = "Revenge, Study 1's three items (check)")
status_of <- function(rev, rival, sample, family) {
  # The hypothesis each row belongs to: H10 (correlations) or H9 (endorsement)
  # in the whole sample, and H11, which repeats them among retributivists.
  base <- if (family == "A") "H10" else "H9"
  hyp <- if (sample == "Whole sample") base else paste0("H11: ", base, " among retributivists")
  # Where the registered test on the registered just-deserts score is found.
  where <- if (sample == "Whole sample") "Table S12" else "Table S17"
  if (rival == "severity_deserts")
    return(paste0("exploratory: new score, not preregistered, reruns no registered test; ",
                  "two-sided only",
                  if (rev == "revenge3") "; revenge on Study 1's three items (check on the revenge scoring)" else ""))
  if (rev == "revenge3")
    return(paste0("exploratory: revenge on Study 1's three items (check on the revenge scoring); ",
                  "registered direction of ", hyp, " kept"))
  if (rival == "just_deserts")
    return(paste0("registered hypothesis and direction (", hyp, "), on the paper's ",
                  "just-deserts score, which was not registered; the registered test uses ",
                  "the registered just-deserts score (", where, ")"))
  # Desert theory rows: the hypothesis names just deserts, so these rows are
  # the hypothesis rerun with desert theory in its place, as the paper
  # reports them.
  paste0(hyp, " rerun on desert theory in place of just deserts, one-sided in the ",
         "registered direction, as the paper reports it; desert theory was not ",
         "registered; the registered test is in ", where)
}

# --- A. Dependent correlations -------------------------------------------------
SAMPLES <- list("Whole sample" = sc, "Retributivists" = rt)
tests_a <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(SAMPLES), function(s) {
  x <- SAMPLES[[s]]
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(REV_SCORING), function(rv) {
    do.call(rbind, lapply(names(RIVALS), function(h) {
      cbind(family = "Correlation with punitiveness: revenge vs rival (Steiger Z, Zou CI)",
```
